name: United States
intro:
American slang is the most widely exported informal vocabulary on earth, which is exactly what makes it hard to pin down. A term can be current in Atlanta, stale in Los Angeles and only just arriving in London, all in the same month. Much of what the rest of the world hears as generic "American" slang originated in African American Vernacular English and reached the mainstream through music, sport and, more recently, social platforms — a route worth knowing, because it explains why so many terms carry a history that their casual users are unaware of.

The entries below favour vocabulary with some staying power over whatever is peaking this week. Where a term has a specific regional home, or a specific origin that changes how it lands, we say so.
metaDescription: American slang explained: 50 common US slang words and phrases with definitions, pronunciation, example sentences and notes on where each term is actually used.

name: United Kingdom
intro:
British slang is unusually stratified. Class, region and age all leave fingerprints on it, and a word that reads as warm in Newcastle can read as sarcastic in Surrey. The country is small enough that speakers are broadly aware of each other's vocabulary and large enough that they rarely use it — most Britons can recognise far more slang than they would ever say out loud.

A recurring trap for visitors is understatement. A good deal of British informal speech means considerably more, or considerably less, than it literally says, and several entries below exist mainly to flag that gap.
metaDescription: British slang explained: 50 UK slang words and phrases with meanings, pronunciation, real example sentences and notes on region, class and tone.

name: Australia
intro:
Australian slang runs on two engines: shortening and irony. Almost any word can be clipped and given an -o or -ie ending, and the results are productive rather than fixed — speakers coin new ones on the spot and expect to be understood. The second engine is a habit of naming things by their opposite, which is why the tallest person in the room may be called Shorty.

Australians also use a small set of terms far more often than outsiders expect, and a larger set far less often than films suggest. Where a word belongs firmly in the second group, the entry says so rather than pretending otherwise.
metaDescription: Australian slang explained: 50 Aussie slang words and phrases with meanings, pronunciation, example sentences and honest notes on which ones locals actually say.

name: Canada
intro:
Canadian slang is often described as a mild variant of American slang, which undersells it. Canada has its own institutional vocabulary — terms from its currency, its school system, its winters and its coffee chains — plus two strong regional varieties that sound nothing alike: Toronto's multicultural youth slang, heavily influenced by Caribbean and Somali speech, and the older vocabulary of Atlantic Canada.

Bilingualism leaves marks too. Several everyday Canadian English words are straight borrowings from Quebec French, used by speakers who have no idea of their origin.
metaDescription: Canadian slang explained: 50 Canadian slang words and phrases with meanings, pronunciation, example sentences and notes on Toronto, Prairie and Atlantic usage.

name: Mexico
intro:
Mexican Spanish carries what is probably the densest slang vocabulary in the Spanish-speaking world, and the single most important thing to understand about it is register. The same word can be an insult, a term of endearment or a filler particle depending on tone and on who is in the room. Getting this wrong is the classic learner's mistake: the vocabulary is easy to acquire and easy to misuse.

A second feature is layering. Many terms carry an innocuous surface meaning and a second, cruder one underneath — the basis of albúr, the Mexican tradition of double-meaning wordplay. Where an entry below has that second layer, we flag it.
metaDescription: Mexican slang explained: 50 Mexican Spanish slang words and phrases with meanings, pronunciation, example sentences with English translations and register warnings.

name: Spain
intro:
Spanish from Spain is noticeably blunter than most Latin American varieties. Words that would be shocking in Bogotá or Lima are ordinary conversational furniture in Madrid, and speakers swear casually and often without any intent to offend. Learners who arrive from a Latin American classroom usually find this the hardest adjustment.

The entries below mark clearly where a term is peninsular-only, because a large share of Spain's slang is genuinely not portable — using it in Mexico or Argentina will get you a blank look at best.
metaDescription: Spanish slang from Spain explained: 50 peninsular Spanish slang words and phrases with meanings, pronunciation, example sentences and English translations.

name: Italy
intro:
Italy unified its language relatively recently, and its slang still shows the seams. A great deal of what passes for Italian slang is regional dialect that escaped its home city — Roman and Neapolitan words in particular have spread nationwide through film and television while keeping an audible local flavour.

Italian also makes heavy use of gesture and intonation, and several entries below are words whose meaning is carried almost entirely by delivery. Where that is the case, the usage notes matter more than the definition.
metaDescription: Italian slang explained: 50 Italian slang words and phrases with meanings, pronunciation, example sentences with English translations and regional notes.

name: France
intro:
French slang has a structural quirk no other language on this site shares: verlan, the practice of reversing a word's syllables to make a new one. Fête becomes teuf, femme becomes meuf, and a few verlan words have been reversed a second time. It is productive, generational, and it means that knowing standard French gets you only part of the way.

The other major source is argot from Paris and Marseille, plus a steady stream of borrowings from Arabic through the banlieues. The entries below note which stream a word comes from, because it tells you a great deal about who says it.
metaDescription: French slang explained: 50 French slang words and phrases with meanings, pronunciation, verlan origins, example sentences and English translations.

name: Japan
intro:
Japanese slang is shaped by a feature the language has and most others do not: an obligatory politeness system. Every sentence already encodes how the speaker ranks themselves against the listener, so slang in Japanese is rarely just a word choice — it is a declaration that the formal register has been switched off, and using it with the wrong person is a social error before it is a vocabulary one.

The productive machinery is worth learning on its own. Nouns become verbs with a -ru ending (Google becomes ググる), adjectives contract in speech (すごい becomes すげー), and long compounds shorten to four syllables (コストパフォーマンス becomes コスパ). Learn those three patterns and a great deal of what looks like new slang turns out to be a word you already know, wearing a shorter coat.

Every entry below is given in Japanese script with a Hepburn romanization, because a word you cannot type is a word you cannot look up.
metaDescription: Japanese slang explained: common Japanese slang words and phrases in kanji and kana with romanization, meanings, example sentences and notes on when each one is rude.

name: South Korea
intro:
Korean slang turns over faster than that of any other language on this site, and it does so by a single dominant mechanism: abbreviation. Take the first syllable of each word in a phrase, stick them together, and you have a new term — 치킨 plus 맥주 gives 치맥, 멘탈 plus 붕괴 gives 멘붕. Whole sentences compress into four letters this way, which is why a Korean twenty-year-old's messages can be unreadable to their own parents.

The second thing to understand is that Korean address terms are not optional decoration. Oppa, unni, sunbae and the rest are used constantly and carry real information about age, gender and hierarchy; several of the entries below are address terms rather than vocabulary, because getting them wrong is the mistake foreigners make first and most often.

Entries are given in Hangul with a Revised Romanization reading, and note where a term is internet-only rather than something you would say out loud.
metaDescription: Korean slang explained: common Korean slang words and phrases in Hangul with romanization, meanings, example sentences and notes on age, hierarchy and when not to use them.

name: Colombia
intro:
Colombia has no single slang. The mountains split the country into speech communities that developed largely out of earshot of each other, and the differences are audible in the first sentence: a paisa from Medellín hangs pues on the end of every clause, a bogotano says usted to his own children, and a costeño from Barranquilla drops consonants at a rate that the interior finds hard to follow. Roughly a third of the entries below are marked for region because using them outside it would be a costume rather than a sentence.

The layer that travelled furthest is parlache, the vocabulary that grew in Medellín's hillside neighbourhoods during the worst years of the drug conflict and then spread nationwide through music and television. Parce, parche and gonorrea all came from there, and they did not arrive neutral — the first two lost their associations completely, the third did not. That is the general trap here: Colombian slang is warm and sounds easy, and a good deal of it carries a class or regional charge that native speakers hear instantly and visitors do not. Where an entry has one, we say so.
metaDescription: Colombian slang explained: 50 Colombian Spanish words and phrases with meanings, pronunciation, regional notes from Medellín to the coast, and English examples.

name: Cuba
intro:
Cuban Spanish has been shaped by three forces that no other variety combines. The first is the Afro-Cuban substrate: words carried over in the ritual languages of Santería and of the Abakuá societies — asere, aché, bembé, ambia — which moved outward from religious and street use into ordinary speech, some of them only in the last forty years. The second is the Revolution and the economic collapse that followed it, which generated an entire working vocabulary for scarcity: resolver, luchar, por la izquierda, sociolismo, el paquete. These are not colourful expressions bolted onto the language; they are the verbs Cubans use to describe what they did this morning. The third is the diaspora, which took a 1960s snapshot of the island's speech to Miami and then kept developing it separately, so that some words on this list are alive in both places and a few — gusano above all — mean opposite things depending on which side of the Florida Straits you are standing.

What trips outsiders up is mostly register and politics rather than vocabulary. Cuban speech is phonetically fast and heavily clipped — final consonants and whole syllables disappear — and it is far coarser in ordinary company than Mexican or Colombian Spanish, so a visitor calibrated to those varieties will consistently misjudge how hard a word lands. Several of the entries below are also politically weighted: chivatón, gusano and pincho are not neutral descriptions, and using them casually will tell a Cuban something about you that you may not have meant to say. Where a term is island-only, diaspora-only, or dangerous to repeat, we say so.
metaDescription: Cuban slang explained: 50 words and phrases from Havana speech, the Special Period and the Miami diaspora, with meanings, examples and notes on register.

name: Dominican Republic
intro:
Dominican Spanish is spoken fast and stripped down, and most of what makes it hard to follow is phonology rather than vocabulary. Syllable-final /s/ is aspirated or gone entirely — do' cerveza' fría', lo' muchacho' — so plurals survive only in the article, and the /d/ of every -ado participle disappears, giving guillao, desacatao, prendío. In the Cibao valley around Santiago, syllable-final /l/ and /r/ turn into an i: porque becomes poique and verdad becomes veidá. Once you can hear those three rules, a great deal of what sounded like unfamiliar slang turns out to be ordinary Spanish worn smooth.

The vocabulary itself has three layers worth separating. There is the old street lexicon of the capital, organised around the tíguere and his opposite the pariguayo. There is the New York layer, carried back and forth by a diaspora large enough that janguear and dominicanyork are as at home in Washington Heights as in Santo Domingo. And there is the dembow layer of the last decade — teteo, desacatao, viejevo — which has spread through Spanish-language music far beyond the island, and which has already pushed words like bonche into the parents' generation. The entries below say which layer a term belongs to, and flag the ones that are dated, regional or coarser than they look.
metaDescription: Dominican slang explained: 50 Dominican Spanish words and phrases with meanings, pronunciation, example sentences and notes on Santo Domingo, Cibao and dembow usage.

name: Ireland
intro:
Hiberno-English is not standard English with a few local words dropped in. Irish grammar came across with the speakers who switched languages, and much of it is still working: "I'm after eating" is the Irish immediate past built out of English parts, "he does be working late" is a habitual tense English otherwise lacks, and "giving out" is a word-for-word translation of an Irish idiom that has nothing to do with giving. None of this is felt as slang by the people using it, which is exactly why it catches visitors out — the vocabulary can be looked up, the grammar cannot.

The regional splits are real rather than decorative. Cork has langer and the sentence-final boy, the north has wee and melter through Ulster Scots, and Dublin supplies most of what the rest of the country hears on television. Two other things are worth saying plainly: the words tourists arrive expecting — begorrah, top o' the morning — are not spoken here by anyone, and several words that sound merely quaint in print are genuinely coarse in the mouth. The entries below say which is which.
metaDescription: Irish slang explained: 50 Hiberno-English words and phrases with meanings, pronunciation, example sentences and honest notes on region, register and grammar.

name: Germany
intro:
German slang is stratified by geography to a degree that surprises people who learned the language from a textbook. A bread roll is a Schrippe in Berlin, a Semmel in Munich, a Weck in Stuttgart and a Rundstück in Hamburg; the tag question at the end of a sentence is ne in the north, gell in the south and wa in Berlin. Alongside that there is a second axis: the small particles — halt, eben, na, doch — that carry no information at all and do most of the work of sounding like a native. Nobody teaches them, and learners who omit them are understood perfectly and still sound wrong.

Two other layers trip outsiders up. The first is Kiezdeutsch, the urban youth speech built on Turkish and Arabic borrowings — wallah, yalla, Digga — which is now general among German teenagers of every background but sounds absurd from an adult. The second is the English that is not English: a Handy is a phone, a Beamer is a projector, Homeoffice is working from home, and a Shitstorm is a polite enough word for a newsreader. The entries below say which layer a word belongs to, and, for the youth vocabulary, whether people actually say it or whether it merely won a prize.
metaDescription: German slang explained: 50 German slang words and phrases with meanings, pronunciation, regional notes, example sentences and English translations.

name: Russia
intro:
Russian slang is organised around one thing above all others: мат, the closed set of four taboo roots — хуй, пизда, ебать and блядь — from which the language builds an enormous, fully grammatical vocabulary. This is not swearing in the English sense of a handful of shock words. The roots take ordinary Russian prefixes and suffixes and generate verbs, adjectives, adverbs and abstract nouns that cover meanings with nothing rude about them at all: охуеть is to be astonished, заебался is exhausted, наебать is to defraud, похуй is not caring. A speaker can run a whole narrative on mat and be perfectly precise throughout. Against that sits an equally elaborate euphemistic layer, built by keeping the entire word-shape and swapping only the offending root — блин for блядь, капец for пиздец, офигеть for охуеть, забить with the taboo noun silently deleted. Knowing which grade of a word you are hearing is most of what register means in Russian.

The other two forces are historical and recent. Decades of the Soviet penal system pushed camp argot — фе́ня — into ordinary speech, so that words like беспредел, косяк, ксива and по понятиям are now said by people who have never been near a prison, usually without knowing where they come from; зашквар, currently a teenage word for anything shameful, has a prison origin most of its users would be startled by. Meanwhile молодёжный сленг absorbs English wholesale and russifies it on contact: a borrowed verb arrives with the -ить ending already attached, so чилить, флексить and гуглить conjugate and take aspect prefixes like any native verb, which is why this layer sounds domestic within months rather than decades. The trap for outsiders is not comprehension but calibration. Mat is an administrative offence in public and unbroadcastable, and a foreigner deploying it — especially a foreigner who has learned it from song lyrics — sounds either menacing or absurd. Understand the whole system; speak the euphemisms.
metaDescription: Russian slang explained: mat and its euphemisms, prison-camp words in everyday use, and russified English, with Cyrillic terms, romanization and example sentences.
